# Relationships

First-class relationships between concepts, modules, invariants, and domains in
this system — especially the **non-obvious** ones that are not visible from
imports, types, or names.

Structural links (who imports whom, who defines what) already live in the code
graph (`diagrams/code-graph.*`) and the symbol index (`diagrams/code-symbols.json`).
**Do not duplicate them here.** This file captures connections that require
understanding to see: shared invariants, implicit contracts, cause/effect across
modules, hidden coupling, and cross-domain analogies.

Each relationship is a self-contained entry so it can stand on its own and be
retrieved independently.

## Relationship template

```
### <A> ⇄ <B>
- Type: shared-invariant | implicit-contract | cause-effect | data-flow | hidden-coupling | analogy
- Relationship: how A and B are connected
- Why it matters: what breaks or gets misunderstood if this link is missed
- Evidence: files / symbols
- Confidence: low | medium | high
- Non-obvious: yes | no   (yes = not derivable from imports, types, or names)
```

## Relationships

### task-store ⇄ http-router
- Type: shared-invariant
- Relationship: the in-memory `Map` in `src/store.js` is the single source of truth for tasks; every route handler mutates tasks only through the store's functions
- Why it matters: if a handler mutates task objects directly instead of going through the store, list/get/update results diverge and the "single source of truth" guarantee breaks
- Evidence: src/store.js, src/router.js
- Confidence: high
- Non-obvious: yes

### in-memory-store ⇄ process-lifecycle
- Type: cause-effect
- Relationship: all task state lives in process memory, so it is created empty on start and lost on stop/restart
- Why it matters: anyone relying on persistence will lose data on redeploy; persistence is a deliberate non-feature of this demo
- Evidence: src/store.js
- Confidence: high
- Non-obvious: yes
